# Diagnosing a No-Crank Condition: Starter vs. Alternator on a 2006 Honda Civic

When a vehicle transitions from cranking weakly to delivering a single click, the diagnostic path shifts rapidly from fuel or ignition issues to the starting circuit itself. In this specific case involving a 2006 Honda Civic EX 1.8L, the symptom progression—weak crank followed by total failure to engage—is a classic signature of thermal expansion in the starter motor rather than an alternator fault.

The initial confusion regarding battery health is common. A month ago, replacing the battery didn't resolve the issue because the root cause wasn't voltage capacity but rather current delivery resistance or mechanical drag within the starter. The fact that the car required a jump to start initially suggests the new battery had sufficient cold cranking amps (CCA), but the starter was unable to draw enough current to overcome internal friction or a worn brush set. When the vehicle eventually stopped cranking entirely, leaving only an audible click, it indicated the solenoid was engaging but the motor itself was locked up.

The critical clue lies in the update regarding heat sensitivity: "It was going bad and would fail when it got hot." This points directly to a failing starter motor or its internal wiring harness. As the starter operates, current flows through heavy-gauge cables and the armature. If there is excessive resistance due to corrosion on terminals or worn brushes, electrical arcing generates localized heat. In a healthy system, this dissipates quickly. In a degraded system, the temperature rises until the windings expand enough to seize mechanically or the internal contacts melt, cutting power before the engine can turn over.

The alternator is almost certainly not the culprit here. An alternator's primary role is to charge the battery and power accessories while the engine runs. If the alternator were completely failed, you might see a dead battery or dim lights after driving, but it does not prevent the starter from engaging when the key is turned. The user noted that all electronics work fine; this confirms the alternator and voltage regulator are likely functioning, as they power the dashboard and accessories even with the engine off (drawing from the battery).

To verify a failing starter without immediately replacing parts, you can perform a load test using a multimeter or by checking for voltage drop across the solenoid terminals. If the vehicle has been driven recently before the failure, let it sit for an hour. If the issue is thermal, the starter might function after cooling down. This "intermittent" behavior is distinct from a battery that dies overnight; batteries fail due to chemical depletion or sulfation over time, not typically immediate heat cycles unless they are severely frozen or damaged.

The single click sound confirms the solenoid coil is receiving power and creating a magnetic field strong enough to pull the pinion gear out. However, if the pinion cannot mesh with the flywheel teeth due to lack of torque from the motor internals, you hear the click but no rotation. This mechanical lock-up under load is definitive for a bad starter on this platform.

Replacing the battery again would be a waste of money until the starter is swapped out. The system requires a component that can handle high-amperage bursts reliably. Once the starter is replaced, the vehicle should start immediately and run normally, assuming no other underlying electrical resistance exists in the ground straps or battery cables.
